title: The Cry from the Depths
english: the grass of the roofs are those who have leaped over

Not as one ascending, but finding no one able to help, he cries to God. Along with confessing where he has fallen, he says, 'Out of the depths I have cried to you, Lord; Lord, hear my voice; for having heard, you will raise me up from the depth of wickedness and the deepest pit' (Ps 130:1-4). This expression agrees with what is said by him later: 'If iniquity be observed, Lord, Lord, who shall stand?' (Ps 130:4).

It is possible even for one dwelling in the earthly place, through human life, to send up this prayer, feeling himself far below both heaven and God; for heaven is high and earth is deep. It is also possible for the one praying to be holy according to what was previously stated. For he does not send up the prayer concerning small and earthly things, but large and heavenly things. He does not send up the prayer from a psychic discourse concerning them, asking for them, but being enlightened by the Spirit, searching all things, and knowing and contemplating the depths of God. Following the one searching these things by the Spirit, it is necessary from these depths to cry to God, deeming himself worthy of having his voice heard. And from these depths he cries, seeking not the non-sensible but all intelligible things and the Holy Spirit itself.

It is equal to 'Let your words be done' (Luke 1:38) for those attending to 'Incline your ear to my voice' (Ps 40:5). Since our voice does not reach the heights, and because there is a great difference in the nature of your words. And from here we learn, having understood, that they are not always the same, but 'Let it be done' also signifies a certain relation. For the words of God do not simply become, but become worthy of attending to Him. Following this, one must also understand what was said concerning Christ: that He became to us wisdom from God (1 Cor 1:30), and that God made Him both Lord and Christ, and such things. Since from you is the propitiation (Rom 3:25), the one being propitiated and, having forgiven sins, [is] Savior, not—
